content: Connective tissue is one of the four primary tissue types in traditional classifications, alongside epithelial, muscle, and nervous tissues. It is primarily defined by exclusion rather than a precise definition, but most tissues in this category share certain characteristics. These include their involvement in structural support, their usual derivation from mesoderm, and their composition, which is largely influenced by the properties of non-living extracellular components. Blood, cartilage, and bone are generally considered connective tissues. However, due to their significant differences from other connective tissues, the term connective tissue proper is often used to exclude these three. Additionally, embryonic connective tissues are sometimes classified separately and will be treated as a distinct category here. Notably, when heated to 190 degrees Fahrenheit, connective tissue emits a vinegar-like odor. Classification of Connective Tissue Connective Tissue Proper Areolar (or loose) connective tissue: This type of tissue holds organs and epithelial layers in place. It contains a variety of protein fibers, including collagen and elastin. Dense connective tissue (or fibrous connective tissue): This tissue forms ligaments and tendons. It is characterized by densely packed collagen fibers, which provide significant tensile strength. Specialized Connective Tissues Blood: Blood functions as a transport medium. Its extracellular matrix, known as blood plasma, carries dissolved nutrients, hormones, and carbon dioxide (in the form of bicarbonate). The primary cellular component of blood is red blood cells. Bone: Bone constitutes nearly the entire adult vertebrate skeleton. Cartilage: In cartilaginous fish (chondrichthyes), cartilage forms the entire skeleton. In most other vertebrates, cartilage is primarily found in joints, where it provides cushioning. The extracellular matrix of cartilage is predominantly composed of collagen. Adipose tissue: This tissue contains adipocytes, which serve functions such as cushioning, thermal insulation, lubrication (notably in the pericardium), and energy storage. Reticular connective tissue: This tissue consists of a network of reticular fibers (fine collagen, type III) that form a soft framework to support lymphoid organs, including lymph nodes, bone marrow, and the spleen. Embryonic Connective Tissues Mesenchymal connective tissue: Found in the developing embryo. Mucous connective tissue: Another type of embryonic connective tissue. Fiber Types in Connective Tissue Connective tissue contains three main types of fibers: Collagenous fibers: Provide strength and structure. Elastic fibers: Allow for flexibility and elasticity. Reticular fibers: Form supportive networks, particularly in lymphoid organs. Disorders of Connective Tissue Several disorders affecting connective tissue have been identified, with both genetic and environmental causes: Marfan syndrome: A genetic disorder caused by abnormalities in fibrillin. Scurvy: A condition resulting from dietary vitamin C deficiency, leading to defective collagen synthesis. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS): A group of genetic disorders characterized by defective type III collagen. Different types of EDS affect various parts of the body, such as joints, heart valves, organ walls, and arterial walls. Loeys-Dietz syndrome: A genetic disorder related to Marfan syndrome, with a focus on vascular deterioration. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum: An autosomal recessive hereditary disease caused by calcification and fragmentation of elastic fibers, affecting the skin, eyes, and cardiovascular system. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): A chronic, multisystem inflammatory disorder of probable autoimmune origin, predominantly affecting young women. Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease): A genetic disorder caused by insufficient production of high-quality collagen, leading to fragile bones. Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva: A rare genetic disorder in which connective tissue is progressively replaced by bone due to a defective gene. Spontaneous pneumothorax: A collapsed lung, believed to be associated with subtle abnormalities in connective tissue. Sarcoma: A neoplastic process originating in connective tissue. Staining of Connective Tissue For microscopic examination, most connective tissue staining techniques highlight tissue fibers in contrasting colors to enhance visualization.
